Labowa Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Łabowa, Poland

Not demolished. Łabowa, first mentioned in 1431, saw individual Jewish families as early as 1765 (9 people); the Stadnicki family's 1801 purchase of the village and subsequent trade privileges encouraged wider Jewish settlement, reaching 362 by the 1880s and 25% of the population (about 250 households) by 1930. A wooden synagogue was built in 1805; by 1938, 461 people belonged to the kehilla. Wartime brought a labor camp to the village; in 1940, Jews were deported to nearby ghettos (Nowy Sącz, Stary Sącz, Rabka, Mszana Dolna) and onward to Bełżec, Treblinka, and Płaszów in 1942. This cemetery, established alongside the local Jewish community in the early 19th century and shown on an 1846 map (oldest tombstone dated 1838), separated the community's leaders in a dedicated hillside section (69 matzevot) from the main burial area (157 matzevot). Restoration began in 1982, funded by descendants, with fencing, a memorial obelisk, and concrete-mounted tombstones; Leo Gatterer of Dobra funded a newer decorative iron gate, and information boards were added in 2020.
